source.title: Exceeding chance level by chance: The caveat of theoretical chance levels in brain signal classification and statistical assessment of decoding accuracy

confidence_rationale: Directly validates the single most important design choice in Q-092's confirming signature -- that held-out accuracy must be tested against an EMPIRICAL PERMUTATION NULL rather than a theoretical 50% chance level. The demonstration is quantitative and adversarial (random Gaussian signals reaching 70%+ two-class accuracy at small n), so it constrains Q-092's episode budget as well as its statistics. High confidence: the result is methodological and machine-independent, so domain transfer risk is nearly nil.
failure_signatures: If Q-092 is run with a small number of held-out episodes, an accuracy well above 50% is expected under the null and reporting it against theoretical chance would manufacture a false PASS.

The permutation null controls for small-sample inflation but NOT for a genuine confound shared by the two conditions -- clearing this null is necessary and explicitly insufficient for Q-092's verdict.

mapping.source_claim_statement: Classification of pure random (Gaussian) signals yields decoding accuracies of up to 70% or higher in two-class problems with small sample sets, because the variance of the observed correct-classification rate scales inversely with sample size; valid inference therefore requires binomial or permutation-based p-values that account for sample size rather than comparison against a theoretical chance level.
mapping.ree_translation: Q-092's confirming signature requires held-out classification of reef-ON vs reef-OFF to exceed a LABEL-PERMUTATION NULL at p<0.05, not to exceed 50%. This paper is the methodological warrant for that choice, and it converts the requirement from a stylistic preference into a hard precondition: with the episode counts typical of REE runs, a theoretical-chance comparison would be actively misleading. It also implies an episode-budget constraint on the experiment design that Q-092's what_would_answer does not yet state numerically.
mapping.mapping_caveat: The paper is about brain-signal classification; Q-092 classifies behavioural trajectory-segment features from a simulated agent. The statistical argument is domain-general (it concerns the sampling distribution of accuracy, not neural data), so transfer is safe -- but the paper says nothing about the OTHER two guards Q-092 specifies (matched untrained-policy control, orthogonal-perturbation specificity), and must not be read as validating the design as a whole.
mapping.source_context: Simulation study on random Gaussian signals plus EEG/MEG decoding examples; two-class and multi-class, varying sample size.

confidence_components.notes: Transfer risk near zero: this is a statement about the sampling distribution of a classification accuracy, which is indifferent to whether the features are neural or behavioural. Mapping fidelity high but not 1.0 because it validates one of Q-092's three guards, not the composite design.
